clue.text: Slow to drop unscrupulous regular string pulling and chicanery

indicators.note: the word Slow is told to let go of a piece, leaving only its first letter

parts.note: low behaviour is base and unscrupulous
playfully, routine plucking of a harp's strings is rehearsal on that instrument

explanation.surface: Someone slow to drop a crooked habit of manipulating people behind the scenes and cheating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'String pulling' looks like influence-peddling; here it is plucking harp strings, done regularly as rehearsal.
explanation.definitionFit: Underhand dealing that is dishonest though perhaps not illegal is a close synonym of trickery and deceit.

clue.text: Man's inspiring review of holiday area's lost retreats

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the man's letters take the others inside

parts.note: Man's read as 'he is', contracted

indicators.note: a review reworks material, so the letters that follow are rearranged
the area is lost, so its abbreviation leaves the word holiday

parts.note: A is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A man's write-up of a holiday region whose secluded getaways have vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' looks like praise for the review, but it means breathing in: the man's contraction takes the other letters inside. 'Lost' drops A before 'review of' jumbles what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Hidden shelters where one can hide away are places of retreat, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Registered web address to describe a country

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for registered, as on a trademark

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so these letters go around the next

parts.note: a URL is the address of a web page

explanation.surface: A registered internet address set up to describe some nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like a noun meaning nation; it is the adjective, as in country life.
explanation.definitionFit: Country as an adjective means of the countryside, a direct synonym of pastoral or agricultural.

clue.text: Did what Nicole Scherzinger did on the circuit more than once?

definitions.text: Did what Nicole Scherzinger did on the circuit more than once?

parts.words: Did what Nicole Scherzinger did on the circuit more than once?
parts.note: the singer repeatedly dated racing driver Lewis Hamilton, so she 'pulled' a speedy man, while the phrase also means to trick someone

explanation.surface: A question about what the pop singer kept doing at the motor-racing track.
explanation.walkthrough: Nicole Scherzinger, of the Pussycat Dolls, had an on-off relationship with Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton; to pull is British slang for attracting a partner.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to deceive or trick someone, and literally here to attract a quick racing man.

clue.text: Fool close to van carrying performers caused trouble

parts.note: an act is a group of performers on a bill

indicators.note: the close, or final letter, goes to the van, or front, of the word for fool

parts.note: to fool someone is to dupe them

explanation.surface: A clown near a removal van holding some actors made a nuisance of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Van' looks like a vehicle but means the vanguard or front; 'close' is the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To misbehave or malfunction is to make trouble, a direct idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: Bigwig to lead on an anecdote collection

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
ana is a collection of anecdotes or sayings about a person

explanation.surface: An important person urged to take charge of a book of stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a verb but is the metal; 'on' merely joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for the most important person in a group, the boss, just as a bigwig is.

clue.text: Toy dog

definitions.meaning: A British brand of die-cast model toy cars
a breed of short-legged Welsh dog, favoured by Queen Elizabeth II

explanation.surface: A small pet breed, the kind called a toy dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the toy brand name and the Welsh dog breed share the name, a double meaning.

clue.text: Deception of crack city job

parts.note: crack, or Irish craic, means fun and good times
NY is New York, the city
a business can be one's job or affair

explanation.surface: Fraud arising from a breach in the city's employment scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like a break-in or drug; it is craic, Irish for fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspicious or underhand activity is a common idiom for trickery and deceit.

clue.text: Hanky-panky? Like one jerking or like one thrusting?

parts.note: jiggery read whimsically as an adjective for jigging or jerking about
pokery read whimsically as an adjective for poking or thrusting

explanation.surface: A suggestive question about whether lovemaking is jerky or thrusting.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves are invented adjectives, the clue's question mark flagging the whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both terms describe dishonest trickery or underhand dealing, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Sign lost from pound sterling — nasty trick!

indicators.note: the letters of the word sign are taken out of the money phrase
something nasty is twisted and unpleasant, so the remaining letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A currency symbol vanishes from British money in a dirty scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing S, I, G, N from POUNDSTERLING leaves POUDTERL, which 'nasty' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret scheme or subsidiary intrigue behind the scenes is a kind of trick or plot.

clue.text: Asian couple at back of romantic place messing around

indicators.note: only the last two letters of the city are turned round
messing the end pair around swaps their order

parts.note: Paris is famed as the city of romance

explanation.surface: An Asian pair in a lovers' city fooling around together.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the final pair IS is swapped, making SI.
explanation.definitionFit: A Zoroastrian of Persian descent living in India, so a person of Asia.

clue.text: Ultimate in conmen starts to inveigle her into lowering zip

indicators.note: the ultimate letter is the final one of the word conmen
the starts are the first letters of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: Tricksters coax a woman into lowering her zipper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zip' looks like a fastener; it is slang for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for nothing, used in English, just as zip is slang for zero.

clue.text: Judge's sentence of East Londoner will, sparking appeal?

definitions.text: Judge's sentence of East Londoner will, sparking appeal?

parts.words: Judge's sentence of East Londoner will, sparking appeal?
parts.note: a Cockney drops the h, so a judge passing sentence would end an 'earing; the result also means charming

explanation.surface: A court ruling against a Cockney that is bound to prompt an appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: East Londoners, or Cockneys, traditionally drop the H; 'appeal' turns from a legal challenge into charm.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming or lovable, so having appeal that wins affection.

clue.text: Outside hotel, is able to adjust this beacon

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit outside, around the hotel letter
adjusting the words is able alters their order

parts.note: H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone outside a hotel can fix this lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: A Belisha beacon is the flashing orange globe on a pole at a British zebra crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is completed by the word beacon, the street lamp named after minister Leslie Hore-Belisha.

clue.text: Rotating ties aren't popular joke shop purchase

indicators.note: rotating something turns it round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to knit is to tie yarn together
things that bomb flop and fail to please

explanation.surface: Spinning neckties that sell poorly at a novelty shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ties' looks like neckwear but is a verb, knits.
explanation.definitionFit: A small capsule releasing a foul smell is a classic prank item sold in novelty shops.

clue.text: Vixen's crony, one engaged in capers

definitions.meaning: Vixen is one of Santa's reindeer, and so is her teammate
someone who capers or leaps about friskily

explanation.surface: A she-fox's companion involved in escapades.
explanation.definitionFit: A reindeer name alongside Vixen and Dasher; also a person who frolics and skips.

clue.text: Set Australian into popping crease, anticipating an incutting delivery

indicators.note: the built word comes before, anticipating, the last piece
the Australian's letter is set into the jumbled crease
popping suggests bursting about, so the word crease is scrambled

explanation.surface: An Aussie batsman in the popping crease, expecting an in-cutting ball.
explanation.walkthrough: The popping crease and in-cutting delivery are cricket terms; the delivery is a birth by surgical incision.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgical birth through an incision in the abdomen is a delivery by cutting in.

clue.text: Comparatively audacious sermon about fool on the first, taking day off

indicators.note: the shortened sermon goes about, around, the other pieces
the day is taken off the word sermon

parts.note: Mon is short for Monday

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece is written on, after, the other

parts.note: an ass is a fool
I is the Roman numeral one, first

explanation.surface: A cheekier homily about an April fool, taking a day off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool on the first' hints at April Fool's Day; 'taking' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparative meaning cheekier or more impudent, so more audacious.

clue.text: Run and go by sink

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
time elapses when it goes by

explanation.surface: Run past the kitchen basin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like a basin; it is the verb, to fall back.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall back into a worse state, to deteriorate again, is to decline or sink.

clue.text: Potter's game? Winning event that's staged

parts.note: in snooker, where players pot balls, a single game is a frame
to be up is to be ahead or winning

explanation.surface: A snooker player's victorious game turns out to be rigged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potter' suggests the ceramicist or Harry Potter; it is a snooker player.
explanation.definitionFit: A conspiracy staged to make an innocent person look guilty is a contrived event.

clue.text: See 4
Fools students over mass reductions in population, we hear

indicators.note: the student union covers over the mass abbreviation, holding it

parts.note: NUS is the UK National Union of Students
m is the symbol for mass in physics

indicators.note: flags that the next word is identified by its sound

parts.note: culls are selective killings to reduce animal numbers

explanation.surface: Idiot students skip lectures over mass animal slaughter.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound of the population-reducing word is spelt KULLS here, completing the dunces' heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupid people, dunces or blockheads, which is what fools are.

clue.text: Swaggering male set up Soho scams without clothes

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the letters read upward, backwards
stripped of their outer letters, the words keep only the insides

explanation.surface: A cocky man organised naked frauds in Soho.
explanation.walkthrough: Soho is a London district known for nightlife; the stripped words give OH and CAM, reversed together.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggressively masculine and showing off, as a swaggering man is.

clue.text: A little mischief on parking space for cabbies

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
a taxi rank is where cabs wait

explanation.surface: Minor naughtiness in a taxi parking bay.
explanation.definitionFit: A practical joke is a small bit of mischief or trickery.

clue.text: Set of three April fools

indicators.note: the word April is fooled with, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A trio of practical jokers on April Fool's Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fools' looks like a noun; it is a verb acting on April.
explanation.definitionFit: A card-game term for three of a kind, from pair royal, so a trio.

clue.text: So good around pervert

parts.note: sic is Latin for thus or so

indicators.note: around means turned round, read backwards

parts.note: OK means good or fine

explanation.surface: So a decent person surrounds a deviant.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a sick or deviant person, a twisted individual or degenerate.

clue.text: I collected rent for Peter Rachman?

indicators.note: the jumbled words collect, take in, the I
rent means torn apart, so the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A landlord boasts of gathering rent for Peter Rachman.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Rachman was a notorious London slum landlord of the 1950s; 'rent' is torn, not money paid.
explanation.definitionFit: A notorious slum landlord exploiting tenants is an example of one making excessive gains.

clue.text: Perfidy of busty woman, old source of comedy

parts.note: a double-D is a large bra cup size
Ealing Studios in west London made famous comedy films in the 1940s and 1950s

explanation.surface: Betrayal by a large-chested woman, from a vintage comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Treachery and duplicity, acting one way while intending another, is a synonym of perfidy.
